title: Starting a Hospice Program in Nebraska: Licensing, Costs, and Step-by-Step Guide

Introduction (2-3 paragraphs)

Starting a Hospice Program in Nebraska represents a meaningful opportunity to serve terminally ill patients requiring comprehensive palliative care while building a compliant, sustainable care business. Oversight and funding are administered by the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) Licensure Unit, with reimbursement and program funding coordinated through Nebraska Medicaid and Medicare for eligible beneficiaries.

With a market signal showing providers are concentrated in urban centers like Omaha and Lincoln, creating significant rural coverage challenges, and reimbursement rates from $190 to $225 per day for routine care, Nebraska offers a market with significant opportunity for providers prepared to navigate licensing, staffing, and compliance requirements. The state’s average gross margin of 83% is notably higher than the national average, indicating strong financial viability for well-run agencies.

This guide walks you through every step of launching a Hospice Program in Nebraska, from regulations and licensing to staffing, reimbursement, and inspections. Whether you aim to serve a bustling urban community or bridge the care gap in a rural county, this comprehensive overview will provide the roadmap you need to succeed.

Table of Contents

  • Understand Nebraska’s Hospice Program Regulations
  • Choose the Type and Size of Your Program
  • Business Structure and Licensing
  • Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan
  • Secure a Suitable Facility or Office
  • Hire and Train Qualified Staff
  • Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans
  • Marketing and Referral Development
  • Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews
  • Frequently Asked Questions

Section 1: Understand Nebraska’s Hospice Program Regulations

Nebraska regulates Hospice Programs through the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) Licensure Unit, which is responsible for the initial licensing and ongoing regulation of hospice programs to ensure they meet state standards for patient care, safety, and operational integrity. Providers serving Medicaid or federally funded populations must also comply with federal frameworks, most notably the Medicare Conditions of Participation (CoPs) and the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA).

The state’s regulatory framework, outlined in the Health Care Facility Licensure Act and detailed in 175 Neb. Admin. Code ch. 16, emphasizes a regulatory theme of comprehensive palliative care, patient and family rights, quality of life, and holistic symptom management. This framework mandates the use of an Interdisciplinary Group (IDG) to develop and manage a patient-centered plan of care. Licenses typically require renewal every 1 to 2 years, though providers must verify the exact term with the DHHS Licensure Unit.

Navigating these state and federal rules is the foundation of a successful hospice agency. A deep understanding of 175 Neb. Admin. Code ch. 16 is not just a suggestion—it’s a requirement for passing your initial licensure survey and maintaining compliance long-term.

Section 2: Choose the Type and Size of Your Program

Nebraska supports multiple hospice service models and levels of care, each with different licensing, staffing, and reimbursement requirements. While all are governed under a single hospice license, your agency must be equipped to provide the four federally mandated levels of care:

  • Routine Home Care (RHC): The most common level of care, provided in the patient’s place of residence (private home, assisted living, or nursing facility). This includes nursing, aide services, social work, and spiritual support.
  • Continuous Home Care (CHC): Provided during a period of crisis to manage acute symptoms. This involves intensive, round-the-clock nursing care at the patient’s residence for a short duration.
  • General Inpatient Care (GIP): For pain or symptom management that cannot be handled in another setting. This requires a contract with a hospital or skilled nursing facility for short-term inpatient care.
  • Inpatient Respite Care: Short-term inpatient care provided in a contracted facility to give the patient’s primary caregiver a break. Medicare allows for up to five consecutive days of respite care.

Beyond these required levels, strategic providers can find success by focusing on niche markets. Program size is not defined by beds but by your agency’s Average Daily Census (ADC) and service area. Capacity typically ranges from small, community-focused agencies serving a single county to larger organizations covering multiple regions. Demand is strongest in Omaha and Lincoln, but these markets are also the most competitive. In contrast, rural areas of Nebraska may offer significant entry opportunities with less competition, as do specialized niches like:

  • Pediatric Hospice and Palliative Care: Serving children with life-limiting illnesses requires specialized staff training and resources.
  • Rural Home-Based Services: Building an agency specifically designed to overcome the logistical challenges of serving geographically dispersed populations.
  • Culturally Sensitive Care: Developing programs tailored to the unique needs of specific populations, such as Nebraska’s Native American communities.

Section 3: Business Structure and Licensing

Before you can provide care, you must establish a solid legal and administrative foundation. Providers in Nebraska typically operate as a Limited Liability Company (LLC) or a Corporation (S-Corp or C-Corp). Your choice will have implications for liability, taxation, and governance. Regardless of the structure, you must:

  • Register with the Nebraska Secretary of State: Formally establish your business entity within the state.
  • Obtain an EIN from the IRS: An Employer Identification Number is required for tax purposes and to hire employees.
  • Secure required insurance coverage: This includes professional liability (malpractice), general liability, and workers’ compensation insurance.
  • Submit a licensing application to the DHHS Licensure Unit: This comprehensive application package will include your business formation documents, proof of financial viability, key personnel information, and draft policies and procedures.

Licensing timelines in Nebraska, including the crucial step of Medicare certification, generally range from 9 to 15 months. This timeline is heavily dependent on your readiness, the completeness of your application, and your ability to pass the subsequent licensure and certification surveys. Delays are common, so meticulous preparation is key.

Section 4: Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A robust business plan is your blueprint for success, guiding your operational strategy and financial projections. Startup costs for a hospice in Nebraska typically range from $200,000 to $600,000. This capital covers initial salaries, office setup, electronic health record (EHR) system implementation, legal and consulting fees, and operational cash flow before reimbursements begin.

Operating expenses are driven primarily by staffing, which represents 50-65% of total costs in a typical hospice agency. This is due to the federally mandated Interdisciplinary Group (IDG) that must include a physician, nurse, social worker, and counselor.

Your revenue will be based on a per diem reimbursement model. Typical reimbursement or revenue ranges in Nebraska include:

  • Routine Home Care (Medicaid/Medicare): Approximately $190 – $225 per day.
  • Gross Margins: Nebraska hospices see an average gross margin of 83%, which is revenue minus direct patient care costs like nursing visits and medical supplies.
  • Break-Even Point: Most new agencies can expect to reach their break-even point within 12 to 18 months of operation, depending on how quickly they can build their Average Daily Census (ADC).

Providers operating at a sustainable Average Daily Census (a key utilization metric for hospice) generally achieve net profit margins in the 5-15% range after accounting for all administrative and overhead costs. Your business plan should project the ADC needed to achieve profitability based on your specific cost structure.

Section 5: Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

While hospice care is delivered in the patient’s home, your agency requires a professional administrative office that serves as the hub for all operations. This facility must be compliant with local zoning and state regulations. Key facility requirements include:

  • A secure, professional office space that protects patient and employee privacy.
  • HIPAA-compliant storage for patient records, including locked cabinets for physical files and secure servers or cloud storage for electronic health records (EHR).
  • A dedicated, confidential space for the Interdisciplinary Group (IDG) to hold meetings and discuss patient care.
  • Private areas for family consultations, staff training, and interviews.
  • Secure storage for any medical supplies or durable medical equipment (DME) your agency manages directly.

Your location selection should consider accessibility for your staff, proximity to key referral sources like hospitals and physician offices, and the geography of your intended service area. For agencies serving rural Nebraska, a strategically located central office is critical for efficient coordination.

Section 6: Hire and Train Qualified Staff

Your team is the heart of your hospice. Federal and state regulations mandate a specific Interdisciplinary Group (IDG) to provide holistic care. Required roles typically include:

  • Medical Director: A licensed physician who provides medical oversight and certifies patient eligibility.
  • Administrator/Director of Nursing: An RN who oversees all clinical and administrative operations.
  • RN Case Managers: Registered nurses who manage the patient’s plan of care and coordinate all services.
  • Medical Social Worker (MSW): A master’s-level social worker who addresses the psychosocial needs of the patient and family.
  • Spiritual Counselor/Chaplain: Provides spiritual support aligned with the patient’s and family’s beliefs.
  • Hospice Aides (CNAs): Certified Nursing Assistants who provide personal care under the supervision of an RN.
  • Volunteer Coordinator: Manages a required volunteer program, which must provide at least 5% of total patient care hours.
  • Bereavement Coordinator: Manages the bereavement program, offering grief support to families for up to 13 months after the patient’s death.

All staff must undergo rigorous background checks and license verification. Training requirements are extensive and must be documented, including an initial orientation covering the hospice philosophy, your agency’s policies, and emergency procedures. All clinical staff must receive ongoing training in pain and symptom management, patient rights, and HIPAA, with annual continuing education mandates to ensure skills remain current.

Section 7: Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Your operational rulebook is your set of policies and procedures. The Nebraska DHHS and Medicare will scrutinize these documents during your licensure survey to ensure they meet all regulatory standards. Nebraska requires written policies covering, at a minimum:

  • Patient Rights and Responsibilities
  • Admission, Transfer, and Discharge Criteria and Processes
  • Comprehensive Assessment and Plan of Care Development
  • Pain and Symptom Management Protocols
  • Infection Control and Prevention
  • Emergency Preparedness Plan
  • Staffing, Supervision, and Volunteer Management
  • Quality Assurance and Performance Improvement (QAPI) Program
  • Bereavement Care Program for Families
  • Ethical Conduct and Financial Billing Procedures

Individual care or service plans are the cornerstone of hospice. They must be developed by the IDG in collaboration with the patient and family within days of admission. These plans must be documented, regularly reviewed (at least every 15 days), and updated to reflect the patient’s changing needs, all in accordance with Nebraska and federal rules.

Section 8: Marketing and Referral Development

Unlike other businesses, hospice marketing is not about consumer advertising. It’s about building trust and educating the healthcare community. Your referrals will primarily come from professional sources who trust your agency to provide compassionate, reliable care. Referrals typically come from:

  • Hospital discharge planners and case managers
  • Oncologists, cardiologists, pulmonologists, and other specialists
  • Primary care physicians and clinics
  • Skilled Nursing Facilities (SNFs) and Assisted Living Facilities
  • Home health agencies that have patients who are declining and may become hospice-appropriate

Successful providers hire hospice liaisons or community educators to build and maintain these critical relationships. Their job is to educate referral sources on your agency’s services, response times, and quality outcomes. The most effective marketing strategy is demonstrating impeccable compliance, excellent communication with physicians, and positive family testimonials.

Section 9: Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews

Oversight in hospice is continuous. Your agency will be subject to periodic, unannounced inspections from surveying bodies including the Nebraska DHHS Licensure Unit for state compliance and a Medicare-approved accreditation organization (like CHAP or ACHC) or the state survey agency for federal certification.

Inspectors focus heavily on clinical documentation and consistent implementation of policies. Common deficiencies often cited during surveys include:

  • Incomplete, inconsistent, or outdated patient plans of care.
  • Failure to conduct and document comprehensive patient assessments on time.
  • Lack of evidence of IDG coordination and communication.
  • Medication management and reconciliation errors.
  • Insufficient documentation of volunteer activities or aide supervision.

To avoid these pitfalls, you must foster a culture of continuous quality improvement (CQI) and maintain audit-ready documentation at all times. Regular self-audits and mock surveys are essential practices for ensuring your agency is always prepared for a surveyor’s visit.

Section 10: Frequently Asked Questions

How long does it take to open a Hospice Program in Nebraska?

  • The entire process, from business planning to receiving the first patient, typically takes 12 to 18 months. This includes the time needed for business formation, application submission, and passing both the state licensure survey and the separate Medicare certification survey.

What licenses are required?

  • You need a Hospice Program license from the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) Licensure Unit. To receive payment from the vast majority of patients, you will also need to achieve Medicare certification, which involves a separate, rigorous survey process to ensure compliance with federal Conditions of Participation.

What reimbursement is available?

  • Reimbursement primarily comes from the Medicare and Nebraska Medicaid hospice benefits. These programs pay a per diem (daily) rate based on the level of care provided. The most common level, Routine Home Care, pays approximately $190 to $225 per day. Some patients may also have coverage through private insurance plans.

Conclusion

Starting a Hospice Program in Nebraska requires careful planning, a deep understanding of state and federal regulations, and unwavering operational discipline. The market presents a clear opportunity, particularly for providers who are willing to serve rural communities and other underserved populations. Providers who invest in robust compliance systems, hire and train a compassionate and qualified team, and build strong relationships within the healthcare community are positioned for long-term success and the profound reward of providing comfort and dignity at the end of life.
